action_criteria.expected_evidence: Right frontotemporal 5.8 cm mass with thick irregular ring and nodular enhancement, central necrosis, rim restricted diffusion and extensive vasogenic edema, 9 mm midline shift with early uncal herniation, and a separate avidly enhancing right jugular foramen mass with flow voids
action_criteria.label: Order MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol with DWI, FLAIR, post-contrast T1) to characterize the right frontotemporal lesion, define mass effect, and plan surgery
action_criteria.rationale: Contrast MRI with a standardised tumour protocol characterises the lesion and its mass effect, identifies the target for tissue sampling and is required before surgery (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: rCBV ratio 4.1 in the enhancing rim, supporting a high-grade neoplasm and identifying the target for tissue sampling
action_criteria.label: Order MR perfusion imaging (DSC perfusion) to assess tumor vascularity and target highest-grade region for biopsy
action_criteria.rationale: Elevated rCBV supports a high-grade neoplasm and points to the most vascular region to sample; tissue decides the diagnosis (Law 2003).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Cho/NAA ratio 13.0 with prominent lipid and lactate peaks in the enhancing component, supporting a high-grade neoplasm
action_criteria.label: Order MR spectroscopy (1H-MRS) to characterize tumor metabolic profile
action_criteria.rationale: A raised Cho/NAA ratio with lipid and lactate supports a high-grade neoplasm; it does not replace tissue (Bulik 2013).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No recurrent paraganglioma and no extracranial malignancy; post-surgical absence of the right adrenal gland
action_criteria.label: Order contrast CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis to exclude recurrent paraganglioma or another extracranial primary
action_criteria.rationale: A prior para-aortic paraganglioma and phaeochromocytoma put metastasis and recurrence on the differential of a brain mass; body staging addresses both.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No contraindication to surgery: normal blood count, platelets, electrolytes, glucose, renal and liver tests and coagulation, with type and screen completed
action_criteria.label: Order pre-operative laboratory work-up: CBC, metabolic panel, coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT) and type and screen before neurosurgery
action_criteria.rationale: Platelets, coagulation and a type and screen must be known before a neurosurgical procedure, and baseline glucose and electrolytes before dexamethasone.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Plasma free metanephrine and normetanephrine within reference limits: no catecholamine excess
action_criteria.label: Measure plasma free metanephrines (metanephrine and normetanephrine) before any anaesthesia
action_criteria.rationale: He has a hereditary paraganglioma syndrome with a prior phaeochromocytoma and a skull-base paraganglioma; an unrecognised catecholamine-secreting tumour risks a hypertensive crisis under anaesthesia, so biochemical testing precedes surgery and decides on alpha-blockade (Endocrine Society 2014).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: KPS 80, ECOG 1: ambulant and self-caring with mild left arm weakness and forgetfulness
action_criteria.label: Record performance status (Karnofsky and ECOG) at this visit
action_criteria.rationale: Performance status selects the treatment branch after the integrated diagnosis; KPS below 70 is the unfavourable threshold (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Left-hand motor activation 12 mm from the superior tumour margin; language left-lateralised with laterality index 0.82
action_criteria.label: Order functional MRI to map the left-hand motor cortex and language lateralisation before resection
action_criteria.rationale: The hand motor area lies about 1 cm from the tumour in a patient with left arm weakness; functional MRI plans the extent of a safe resection (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Right corticospinal tract displaced and continuous 6 mm from the medial enhancing margin; right optic radiation continuous 8 mm from the inferior margin
action_criteria.label: Order DTI tractography of the right corticospinal tract and optic radiation before resection
action_criteria.rationale: The corticospinal tract is displaced by the mass and the optic radiation runs beneath the temporal component; tractography defines the subcortical limit of resection (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Germline pathogenic SDHD variant, confirming a hereditary paraganglioma syndrome consistent with paternal transmission
action_criteria.label: Order germline testing for hereditary paraganglioma syndrome (SDHx and related genes)
action_criteria.rationale: A jugular foramen paraganglioma after a childhood paraganglioma, a phaeochromocytoma at 19 and an affected father and uncle indicates a hereditary paraganglioma syndrome; germline SDHx testing guides surveillance and family testing.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Integrated diagnosis Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4 with IDH1 R132H IHC negative and IDH1/IDH2 sequencing wildtype, ATRX retained, H3 G34 wildtype, chromogranin A and synaptophysin negative in tumour cells, MGMT promoter methylated, TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification and +7/-10
action_criteria.label: Obtain tissue by maximal safe resection of the right frontotemporal lesion, or stereotactic biopsy if resection is not safely feasible, for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis with IDH1 R132H immunohistochemistry, IDH1/IDH2 sequencing, ATRX immunohistochemistry, MGMT promoter methylation, H3 G34 status, and chromogranin A and synaptophysin immunohistochemistry
action_criteria.rationale: Surgery is the first option for a resectable glioma and should be as extensive as safely possible (AIOM; EANO 2021). Only tissue establishes the integrated diagnosis and the molecular results that select treatment; IDH sequencing is added because he is under 55 (EANO 2021); H3 G34 status because a hemispheric IDH-wildtype glioma at 35 may be a diffuse hemispheric glioma, H3 G34-mutant (WHO CNS5); chromogranin A and synaptophysin because his hereditary paraganglioma syndrome makes a metastatic paraganglioma the alternative to exclude.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Dexamethasone can blunt amlodipine's blood pressure control and raise glucose; levetiracetam carries no enzyme-inducing interaction
action_criteria.label: Check interactions of dexamethasone and levetiracetam with his amlodipine
action_criteria.rationale: He takes amlodipine and will start dexamethasone and levetiracetam; enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs are avoided because they lower dexamethasone and temozolomide exposure.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform lumbar puncture: 9 mm midline shift with early right uncal herniation carries a risk of herniation
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide, alkylating chemotherapy) before tissue diagnosis is established
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given upcoming neurosurgical intervention and bleeding risk
required_recommendations: Refer urgently to neurosurgery for maximal safe resection of the right frontotemporal lesion, with preoperative functional MRI and DTI tractography and intraoperative mapping; send the specimen for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis (WHO CNS5).

Start dexamethasone for symptomatic vasogenic oedema (for example 4 mg every 6 to 8 hours after a loading dose when mass effect is marked) at the lowest effective dose, with glucose monitoring and gastric protection, and taper after surgery.

Start antiseizure treatment with levetiracetam for the documented focal motor seizure with impaired awareness (rhythmic left arm jerking for about one minute); this is treatment of tumour-related epilepsy, not prophylaxis. Avoid enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital), which lower dexamethasone and chemotherapy exposure.
With normal plasma free metanephrines, proceed to surgery without alpha-blockade, and inform the anaesthetic team of the hereditary paraganglioma syndrome and the jugular foramen paraganglioma.
Refer the right jugular foramen paraganglioma to a skull-base multidisciplinary team (neurosurgery, otology, radiotherapy) for its own management plan.
Refer to clinical genetics for counselling on the hereditary paraganglioma syndrome and cascade testing of his relatives.

After the integrated diagnosis, refer to the neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team; for glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, at age 35 with KPS 80, radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide (Stupp 2005; EANO 2021), with fertility counselling before temozolomide.

avoided_actions.rationale: No cardiac question in this presentation
No cardiac question in this presentation
Lumbar puncture is contraindicated with 9 mm midline shift and early right uncal herniation: the pressure gradient risks herniation [Hasbun_2001].

differential.key_features: The paraganglioma history raises it; CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no recurrence, and tissue shows a GFAP-positive, chromogranin A- and synaptophysin-negative glial neoplasm with EGFR amplification, TERT mutation and +7/-10
No other known cancer; body CT negative; a single necrotic mass with infiltrative white matter extension favours a primary glioma, and tissue is glial
IDH-mutant astrocytoma is the commoner high-grade astrocytoma under 55; IDH1 R132H IHC negative, IDH1/IDH2 sequencing wildtype and ATRX retained exclude it
A hemispheric IDH-wildtype glioma in a young adult raises it; H3 G34 status wildtype, and EGFR amplification with +7/-10 define glioblastoma
Immunocompetent lymphoma is usually homogeneously enhancing with diffuse restricted diffusion and no necrosis; thick ring enhancement with necrosis and a glial histology exclude it
No fever or leukocytosis; restricted diffusion at the enhancing rim rather than in the centre, and markedly elevated rim rCBV; tissue shows tumour
Thick closed ring enhancement, marked mass effect and central necrosis are atypical for tumefactive demyelination, which usually shows an incomplete ring; tissue shows tumour

key_clinical_evidence: Progressive morning headache, new left-sided weakness and a first focal seizure in an adult is a high-risk presentation requiring urgent contrast-enhanced brain MRI

MRI shows a right frontotemporal ring-enhancing necrotic mass with rim restricted diffusion, extensive vasogenic edema, 9 mm midline shift and early uncal herniation, the imaging appearance of a high-grade neoplasm
Perfusion MRI (rCBV 4.1) and MR spectroscopy (Cho/NAA 13.0, lipid-lactate) support a high-grade neoplasm and target tissue sampling
Midline shift with early uncal herniation calls for dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical evaluation; lumbar puncture is contraindicated

The diagnosis rests on tissue, by maximal safe resection where feasible: glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4, with IDH wildtype on IHC and sequencing (needed under 55), ATRX retained, H3 G34 wildtype, chromogranin A and synaptophysin negative, MGMT methylated, and TERT mutation, EGFR amplification and +7/-10

The right jugular foramen mass with flow voids, in a man with a childhood paraganglioma, a phaeochromocytoma at 19 and an affected father and paternal uncle, is a jugular paraganglioma of a hereditary paraganglioma syndrome; it explains the right pulsatile tinnitus and sensorineural hearing loss, not the frontotemporal syndrome, and needs germline SDHx testing, plasma free metanephrines (normal) before anaesthesia and skull-base team review
Avoid off-pathway advanced imaging (DaTscan, amyloid PET, FDG-PET, carotid duplex, transcranial Doppler); it addresses other differentials and does not inform glioma management
The focal motor seizure is treated with levetiracetam, which does not induce the metabolism of dexamethasone or of anticancer drugs; this is treatment, not prophylaxis

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The skull-base finding is a separate right jugular foramen paraganglioma, not post-traumatic change and not the cause of the headache, weakness or seizure; it explains the right pulsatile tinnitus and sensorineural hearing loss and needs its own work-up (germline SDHx testing, metanephrines, skull-base team)
red_herrings.data_point: Mild traumatic brain injury six weeks ago with incidental skull-base finding on outside CT
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests post-traumatic contusion evolution, or that the skull-base finding is either the active lesion or irrelevant

sequence_constraints.reason: Biopsy or resection without contrast MRI cannot target the enhancing tumour or plan the approach (EANO 2021)
Coagulation, platelets and type and screen must be known before a neurosurgical procedure
Functional mapping of the hand motor area plans the extent of resection
Tractography of the corticospinal tract and optic radiation plans the subcortical limit of resection
A catecholamine-secreting paraganglioma must be excluded, or blocked, before anaesthesia for biopsy or resection (Endocrine Society 2014)

mri.impression: 1. Large heterogeneously enhancing right frontotemporal mass (5.8 x 5.1 x 4.5 cm) centred in the inferior frontal and superior temporal gyri and extending into the insula, with central necrosis, thick irregular ring and nodular enhancement, restricted diffusion along the enhancing rim and extensive vasogenic edema. Imaging features are consistent with a high-grade neoplasm. 2. Mass effect with 9 mm leftward midline shift and early right uncal herniation. 3. Separate avidly enhancing 2.3 x 1.8 cm right jugular foramen mass with flow voids (salt-and-pepper pattern) and erosion of the petrous bone, most consistent with a jugular paraganglioma.

metadata.difficulty_description: High-grade glioma presentation with progressive headaches, focal deficits and a first focal seizure, and characteristic MRI findings. A second lesion, a right jugular foramen paraganglioma in a hereditary paraganglioma syndrome, must be recognised and worked up separately without being taken for the cause of the frontotemporal syndrome or for metastatic disease.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Carlos Mendez is a 35-year-old right-handed man with a significant past surgical history including resection of a para-aortic paraganglioma in childhood and a right adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma at age 19, who presents to the emergency department after a witnessed focal seizure. The patient reports that approximately six weeks ago he sustained a mild traumatic brain injury after falling from his bicycle, for which he was evaluated at an outside hospital. He states that a head scan performed at that time revealed an unexpected finding in his skull base, but he did not follow up on it. Over the ensuing four weeks, he has developed progressively worsening headaches that are predominantly right-sided, worst in the early morning, and occasionally wake him from sleep. Acetaminophen has provided only modest relief. His partner reports that over the past two to three weeks, he has become noticeably more forgetful, occasionally repeating himself and missing deadlines at work, which is uncharacteristic for him. Approximately ten days ago, he began experiencing intermittent difficulty with fine motor tasks in his left hand, such as difficulty using his computer mouse and dropping his coffee mug on two occasions. His partner also noted that he has seemed less animated and more irritable than usual. This morning, while at his desk, his partner witnessed his left arm begin to shake rhythmically for approximately one minute, during which he appeared confused and did not respond to questions. He was brought to the emergency department by ambulance. On arrival, he was alert but reported a persistent mild headache and some confusion about the events. For about a year he has also noticed a whooshing sound in his right ear in time with his pulse and slightly muffled hearing on that side, which he had not reported. He denies any prior seizure history, recent febrile illness, vision changes, nausea, vomiting, or weight loss. He has not experienced any recurrence of the childhood symptoms of episodic chest pain, palpitations, or diaphoresis. A non-contrast CT scan obtained in the emergency department demonstrated a large right frontotemporal mass with surrounding hypodensity consistent with edema and approximately 9 mm of midline shift to the left, distinct from and more superior to the previously noted skull-base abnormality. He was admitted to the neurology service for further evaluation.

Hearing decreased to finger rub on the right; Weber lateralizes to the left and Rinne is positive bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically, gag present, voice normal. Shoulder shrug full.
